summary:
Akwa Ibom State stands under Nigeria's national criminal framework. Same-sex sexual activity has been illegal across the country since 1916, and the Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014, passed by the House of Representatives on 30 May 2013 and signed by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014, invalidates any marriage or civil union entered into between persons of the same sex and carries a maximum penalty of up to 14 years' imprisonment.

Akwa Ibom lies outside the twelve northern states operating Shari'a-based criminal codes, so the death-penalty layer does not reach it. The ceiling for same-sex sexual activity in Akwa Ibom is 14 years' imprisonment under the secular national statute.

The 2014 Act reaches well beyond marriage. Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice, as reported by Sahara Reporters on 19 August 2026, adds that the Act criminalises participants and guests at same-sex weddings.

Nigeria offers no legal recognition of gender identity, no anti-discrimination protections and no recognition of same-sex relationships. The UK Home Office country policy and information note (June 2025) records countrywide harm patterns of arrests, detention and mob violence against LGBT+ people, and no state-specific enforcement divergence is documented for Akwa Ibom.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Trans people in Nigeria face documented killing and official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; the police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion; an October 2024 investigative panel found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.
tangentialFactors:
The death-penalty layer that does not reach Akwa Ibom is active elsewhere in Nigeria. The UK Home Office (June 2025) records that Shari'a penal codes in the twelve northern states carry penalties for same-sex conduct ranging from lashes or caning up to death by stoning: a Shari'a court in Bauchi sentenced three men to death by stoning in 2022, a further stoning sentence was reported from Bauchi in May 2024, and in January 2014 a mob stormed a Bauchi court demanding death during a sodomy trial. A stoning sentence could not be carried out until ratified by the state governor.

Police violence against perceived gay people is a routine feature of enforcement in the south as well. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law that produces a climate of hostility independent of its text.

Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public. The UK FCDO advisory warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Shari'a law in northern states.
localsOnly:
Residents of Akwa Ibom have no state-level protection machinery: there is no anti-discrimination law, no legal recognition of gender identity and no recognition of same-sex relationships at either national or state level, so gender-marker changes on identity documents have no statutory route.

Enforcement patterns recorded countrywide apply in the state. The UK Home Office documents arrests, detention and mob violence against LGBT+ people across Nigeria, and Human Rights Watch records police use of the 2014 Act to justify torture and arbitrary arrest. No state-specific enforcement divergence is documented for Akwa Ibom, so residents face the same 14-year ceiling and the same arrest exposure as elsewhere in southern Nigeria.

Placement of a transgender prisoner between male and female sections is left to institutional discretion. In the Bobrisky case the authorities' choice of a maximum-security facility was later found to violate the Nigerian Correctional Service Act, but the panel addressed the security classification rather than the question of which sex a trans woman should be held with.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether proposals to criminalise public cross-dressing have been enacted is unresolved by the sources available here; Reuters reported the proposals in September 2022 and no source in this inventory confirms their legislative status.

No Akwa Ibom-specific enforcement data is sourced. The state-level picture rests on the national statute and on countrywide harm patterns, with no documented state divergence and no documented state-level case.

Rules governing gender markers on Nigerian passports and other identity documents, and any screening practice at entry that could disclose a visitor's trans status, are not sourced in this inventory.

Facility access, healthcare provision and hate-crime sentencing provisions specific to Akwa Ibom are not sourced; the inventory records no anti-discrimination protection nationally but does not address state-level hate-crime law.
